this is the make_detections function:
def letterbox_image(img, inp_dim):
    '''resize image with unchanged aspect ratio using padding'''
    img_w, img_h = img.shape[1], img.shape[0]
    w, h = inp_dim
    new_w = int(img_w * min(w/img_w, h/img_h))
    new_h = int(img_h * min(w/img_w, h/img_h))
    resized_image = cv2.resize(img, (new_w, new_h),
                               interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)
    canvas = np.full((inp_dim[1], inp_dim[0], 3), 128)
    canvas[(h-new_h)//2:(h-new_h)//2 + new_h,
           (w-new_w)//2:(w-new_w)//2 + new_w, :] = resized_image
    return canvas


def prep_image(img, inp_dim):
    """
    Prepare image for inputting to the neural network.
    Returns a Variable
    """

    orig_im = img.copy()
    dim = orig_im.shape[1], orig_im.shape[0]
    img = (letterbox_image(orig_im, (inp_dim, inp_dim)))
    img_ = img[:, :, ::-1].transpose((2, 0, 1)).copy()
    img_ = torch.from_numpy(img_).float().div(255.0).unsqueeze(0)
    return img_, orig_im, dim

    if CUDA:

        img = img.cuda()
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(Variable(img), CUDA)
    output = write_results(output, confidence, num_classes,nms=True, nms_conf=nms_thesh)
    im_dim = im_dim.repeat(output.size(0), 1)
    scaling_factor = torch.min(inp_dim/im_dim, 1)[0].view(-1, 1)
    output[:, [1, 3]] -= (inp_dim -scaling_factor*im_dim[:, 0].view(-1, 1))/2
    output[:, [2, 4]] -= (inp_dim - scaling_factor*im_dim[:, 1].view(-1, 1))/2
    output[:, 1: 5] /= scaling_factor

        output[i, [2, 4]] = torch.clamp(output[i, [2, 4]], 0.0,im_dim[i, 1])

    except:

        a=[]

🚀 Feature
Add files to https://download.pytorch.org/whl/ to implement PEP 503 for pip --extra-index-url and for pipenv Pipfile extra source urls.
Motivation
pipenv install using package configuration like torch = {file = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu100/torch-1.1.0-cp36-cp36m-linux_x86_64.whl"} fails with hash mismatch. I guess the problem could be that it downloads the hashes from package releases on pypi and they do not match the whl that provides the package with same name. Pipenv promises vulnerability check in addition to other nice new features for managing package configuration.
Using the simple API you could just document one command that always installs the latest release.
This is related to issue #4793.
Pitch
Rename the different cuda version packages uniquely, like torch-cu100. Add metadata Provides-Dist header to indicate it provides torch to satisfy dependencies on torch.
Provide the simple repository api at URL https://download.pytorch.org/whl/, which lists the different torch-cuNN, torchvision-cuNN etc. packages.
For pip it should work to use pip --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/ torch-cu100 to install latest up to date version of torch for CUDA 10.0.
For pipenv it should work to use configuration like
[[source]]
name = "pytorch"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/"
verify_ssl = true

[packages]
torch = {version="*", index="pytorch"}

Alternatives
Could keep old package names and provide many different simple repository apis for different cuda versions.
However I do not see much need for this, as it is possible to reduce the impact of change by keeping the package names for the cuda version currently on PyPi and just rename the other cuda version packages.
Additional context
I am not experienced in setting up Python repositories, so this requires some testing it surely works.
I think the rename of packages and use of Provides-Dist would be good for upload of all cuda versions to PyPi as well.

🚀 Feature
Move QNNPACK micro kernels under ATen.
Motivation
The initial motivation for this move was born out of an observation in a performance study that revealed Lenet and XRayMobileV3 could benefit from caching qnnpack_create calls.  In caffe2 the cached state is stored as part of the qnnp_operator handle, but in PyTorch we currently create this handle for each operator invocation.   To minimize the performance penalty of doing so, the plan is to factor out as much of this computation to a setup phase, yet defer to runtime the absolute minimum set of computation that was also a design-time computation in Caffe2, but now must be made run-time in PyTorch due to its design.
QNNPACK is currently used both by Caffe2 and PyTorch, and while this modification benefits PyTorch in that it allows use of QNNPACK more optimally, it introduces complexity into the version used by Caffe 2.  Hence the consensus was to move QNNPACK to PyTorch repository with the general long-term goal of seamlessly integrating it into ATen.
Pitch
Move QNNPACK to PyTorch/master with the long-term goal of seamlessly integrating it with ATen.  This includes:

Integrating QNNPACK's build system into PyTorch.
Integrating QNNPACK's test suite with PyTorch's CI.
Stripping down the library to the bare minimum by removing code unused in PyTorch.
Moving towards a C++ implementation.
Reworking the API to be more functional.
Exploring other micro kernel implementations.

Alternatives
Fork the QNNPACK repository and add a second QNNPACK submodule for PyTorch's use only.
cc @jerryzh168 @jianyuh @dzhulgakov

In the following code introduced in version 1.2.0 by #20124, when constructing the _LRScheduler, the step method of optimizer is replaced with a new closure that captures the optimizer itself.

  
    
      pytorch/torch/optim/lr_scheduler.py
    
    
        Lines 29 to 40
      in
      9cb9f15
    
  
  
    

        
          
           # Following https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/20124 
        

        
          
           # We would like to ensure that `lr_scheduler.step()` is called after 
        

        
          
           # `optimizer.step()` 
        

        
          
           def with_counter(func, opt): 
        

        
          
               @wraps(func) 
        

        
          
               def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): 
        

        
          
                   opt._step_count += 1 
        

        
          
                   return func(*args, **kwargs) 
        

        
          
               wrapper._with_counter = True 
        

        
          
               return wrapper

    del scheduler

    print(gc.collect())

_check_driver() uses a term "NVIDIA driver" instead of "CUDA" and confuses users.
NVIDIA driver is obviously NVIDIA video card driver, which has versions like 384.130
CUDA Toolkit has versions like 9.0 and represented as 9000 in int values.
The error message confuses users:

The NVIDIA driver on your system is too old (found version 9000).
Please update your GPU driver by downloading and installing a new
version from the URL: http://www.nvidia.com/Download/index.aspx
Alternatively, go to: https://pytorch.org to install
a PyTorch version that has been compiled with your version
of the CUDA driver.

And should be changed to

CUDA Toolkit on your system is too old (found version 9000).
Please update CUDA Toolkit by downloading and installing a new
version from the URL: https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads
Alternatively, go to: https://pytorch.org to install
a PyTorch version that has been compiled with your version
of CUDA Toolkit.

_check_driver() uses cudaDriverGetVersion underneath and according to the documentation it returns CUDA version(surprise!)
Initially reported in #25581

According to https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/issues/16202#note_140528, we should always pin windows sdk version and the msvc compiler version when possible. Due to our limited infra and staffing, it is impossible to test every combination of MSVC compiler version and Windows SDK. So the solution is to pin these versions on default and check them during configuration. We can provide flags for users to bypass those checks, but then it's the user's responsibility to ensure that they are working.
Actually, I guess this one is the possible root cause of most LibTorch issues on Windows. We tested them and they passed in CI. This is confirmed to fix some issues like #15757 (comment)
